title: Before the Lights Come On
subtitle: An Essay Collection from the Davidson AI Innovation Center

paragraphs: My father did not die because no one knew what was wrong with him. He died because the hospital asked for money we did not have, and they would not move him to the ward until we paid. We gathered what we could — family, neighbours, friends — but it was not enough and it was not fast enough. He died in the hallway of a health facility waiting for money, not medicine.
I tell this story not for sympathy. I tell it because it is the story of almost every family in Oloibiri, and most families will never tell it to anyone who has the power to change anything.

I left medical school when the fees became impossible. I did not stop wanting to understand illness and healing — I simply had no institutional path to pursue that understanding. Then the Davidson AI Innovation Center opened, and I started learning again. Not medicine. Learning itself. How to ask the right questions. How to find information. How to hold a conversation with something that knows more than I do and still remain the one in charge.

sections.heading: What the healthcare navigator does
paragraphs: I now see patients — though that word implies a formality we do not have. People come to me. They describe what is wrong. I use the AI to help me understand: what could this be, what questions should I ask, what do I need to know about this symptom in the context of this person's life?

I am not a doctor. I do not pretend to be a doctor. What I am is someone who can hold the question long enough and carefully enough that the family is not alone with it. In a community with no clinic, no pharmacy, and no resident physician, that is not nothing. That is, in fact, almost everything.

Eight patients in a single week this past month. Malaria. A head injury. A knife wound that needed sutures and a referral. A child with recurring asthma whose family had no idea it had a name. Less than two dollars per consultation on average — not because I charge so little, but because I charge what people have.
My father died in a hallway. I work in a room with four computers and a solar panel. I am not sure this is justice. But I know it is not nothing.

parts.label: Part One: The Idea That Would Not Wait

paragraphs: There was a room. It had been empty for a long time — the kind of empty that gathers dust and purpose at the same time. Michael and I looked at it and did not see what was missing. We saw what could be there.

We found four computers. We found a way to get power from the sun. We found a connection to the internet that made the world small enough to touch. And then we went door to door, and we said: send your children. There is no cost. We want them.
Thirty children came. Some had never used a keyboard. Some had never seen a screen up close. One girl touched the monitor like she was checking if it was real.

sections.heading: Sir, can the computer hear me?
paragraphs: The question came from a boy in the second week. He had been watching others type, and the typing looked impossible to him — his fingers were not certain which key was which, and the cursor moved in ways that confused him. He leaned toward the screen and asked it: can you hear me?
We told him: yes. You can speak to it. And he did.

That was the moment the room became something different from what we had planned. We had planned a computer lab. What we got was a conversation — hundreds of them, every day, between children who had never had access to anything and a technology that could meet them exactly where they were.

The rainy season came. The solar panels struggled. We moved sessions. We borrowed generators. We did not close. You do not close something like this when you have seen what it does to a child to be seen as capable.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Getting It Wrong

paragraphs: I am a mechanical engineer who spent thirty years trying to bring electricity to places that did not have it, under the assumption that electricity was what they were missing. I was not wrong about the value of power. I was wrong about the order of things.

The ETHOS program at the University of Dayton was the most serious attempt I made. We went to communities. We listened. We built systems. We left. And six months later, in too many cases, the systems were not being used — or were being used wrongly, or had failed and no one knew how to fix them, and there was no one nearby who understood them well enough to try.

The Molly Savage study changed what I thought I knew. She documented, systematically, what we had sensed but not measured: the technology outlasted the human capacity to use it. The gap was not watts. The gap was understanding.

sections.heading: The inversion
paragraphs: The thesis I now hold — and that the Davidson AI Innovation Center was built to test — is this: human capability must be developed before the infrastructure arrives, not after. Electrification without education produces dependency. Electrification with education produces agency.
I emailed Renewvia. Nicholas Selby connected me to Bennywhite. Bennywhite said yes before I had finished explaining what I was proposing.

I have never been to Africa. I have funded this from my own retirement savings, because I believe in the inversion and I believe in Bennywhite, and because the data — 71% decline in AI scaffolding demand from month one to month five — suggests I was right about what was missing, and wrong about what to do about it.

chapters.title: We Published the Blueprint in 2022. The Tenant Just Changed.

paragraphs: In late 2022, my colleagues at the University of Dayton, our partners at Synota, and I published a paper — peer-reviewed in Energies the following January — with an unwieldy academic title and a simple premise: the reason solar minigrids fail to attract investment in the world’s poorest communities is not engineering. It’s economics. A village new to electricity uses very little of it, mostly in the evening. The revenue trickles in over decades. No investor waits that long.

Our proposal was to give every minigrid an anchor tenant from day one — a containerized bitcoin mining operation that buys the power the community doesn’t yet use. We called it “impact mining.” The framework had rules that mattered to us more than the mining did: community load gets priority, always. The system is sized to serve people first and machines second. And after the payback period, ownership transfers to the community — including all the extra generating capacity that once fed the miners. In one scenario, we showed a village in Liberia ending up with more than twice the microgrid it would otherwise have had, at $0.10 per kilowatt-hour instead of $0.45.

We weren’t alone in seeing this. Within a year, Gridless — backed by Jack Dorsey’s Block — was proving the model across Kenya, Malawi, and Zambia. In the DRC, Virunga Energies attached mining to the Luviro hydro plant and watched utilization climb from 5% to 50% while household tariffs fell from $0.35 to $0.15 per kilowatt-hour. This spring, Andrew Herscowitz (CEO of the Mission 300 Accelerator), Scott Salandy-Defour (Liquidstar), and Dennis Nderitu (GEAPP) made the general case: digital loads can transform minigrid economics across Africa.
The model works. And yet I now believe the tenant we chose was wrong — or rather, incomplete. Our own paper said so, if you knew where to look.

sections.heading: The warning in our own tables
paragraphs: Every scenario in that 2022 paper carried two numbers: a “bullish” payback and a “bearish” one, reflecting the highs and lows of bitcoin mining rewards. For our Ghana case, that spread was 4.67 years versus 57 years. Same hardware, same sun, same village. The difference was entirely the price of bitcoin.
That is not an investment thesis. That is a coin flip with a solar array attached.

Three years later, the market has rendered its verdict. Mining margins have compressed with each halving, and the large American miners — Core Scientific, TeraWulf, Hut 8 — have been converting their facilities to AI compute, because a GPU earning contracted rates beats an ASIC earning whatever the block reward happens to be worth. By GEAPP’s own arithmetic, AI workloads can earn five to ten times more per kilowatt-hour than mining.
So the anchor-tenant architecture we proposed survives intact. Only the tenant changes.

sections.heading: What America’s data center backlash teaches us
paragraphs: There’s a second reason to look again at this model, and it comes from an unexpected direction: the growing American revolt against data centers.

The complaint is legitimate. Data centers in the US compete with households for constrained grid capacity. They receive favorable power deals, create remarkably few permanent jobs, and residential ratepayers watch their bills climb to fund the transmission buildout. The social contract is: you bear the cost, someone else gets the compute.

Now invert every term. In an off-grid African community, the data center doesn’t strain the grid — it creates the grid. Every kilowatt of capacity the compute underwrites is a kilowatt the community never had. The tariff doesn’t rise; it falls, as Virunga demonstrated. In sun-rich places — Kenya’s Rift Valley, the Sahel, the Niger Delta — the solar resource that makes this viable runs nearly year-round.

But I want to be honest about a risk that travels. The American objection could resurface in African form: foreign-owned machines consuming local power while the village watches from outside the fence. If the community’s only relationship to the compute is proximity, we’ve built extraction with better optics.
Which brings me to the question that actually matters.

sections.heading: The problem bitcoin never had
paragraphs: Bitcoin mining has one genuinely magical property: permissionless revenue. Plug in a machine anywhere on earth and it earns. No customers, no contracts, no sales.

AI compute is not like that. A GPU is an expensive, fast-depreciating asset that only pays for itself at high utilization, serving real workloads for real customers over real connectivity. Swap the ASIC for an H100 and you trade price volatility for demand risk. Decentralized marketplaces like Akash help. Starlink solves the connectivity problem that didn’t have a solution in 2022. But the question every rural AI-compute proposal must answer is brutally simple: who buys the compute?
Here is where I part company with every version of this model I’ve seen — including my own from 2022.

sections.heading: The village that staffs the data center
paragraphs: For the past two years I’ve been working with a community you’ve likely never heard of: Oloibiri, in Bayelsa State, Nigeria — the site of the country’s first oil well, and a place that received almost nothing from the wealth pumped out from under it. With local leadership, we founded the Davidson AI Innovation Center there, and built a learning platform on a principle we call AI that coaches instead of answers. Young people in Oloibiri aren’t consuming AI. They’re becoming AI engineers.

It’s working in the most concrete way I can measure: standout learners are now completing paid, fixed-price AI engineering contracts for a US energy-fintech company. Real deliverables, real invoices, real dollars flowing into a community the grid forgot.

Every distributed-compute model I’ve seen treats the community as a beneficiary of what the machines make possible — cheaper power, AI tutoring, telehealth. All good. But the community’s role is to receive.
Oloibiri suggests the inversion. The community staffs the compute. And that answers the demand question three ways at once:

Contracted work. A trained local workforce wins the kind of remote AI engineering contracts our learners are already delivering — revenue that has nothing to do with crypto prices and everything to do with skills.

Local inference. The coaching platform, and tools like it, generate on-site demand for compute serving education, agriculture, and health — latency-tolerant workloads that suit a village data center perfectly.

Marketplace capacity. Whatever the workforce and platform don’t consume gets sold into decentralized compute markets, with older ASICs kept as interruptible ballast soaking up surplus midday solar — preserving the one thing bitcoin still does best.
The compute anchors the grid. The workforce anchors the compute. That second sentence is what’s been missing.

sections.heading: Education before electricity
paragraphs: For twenty years I’ve watched the development sector sequence things the same way: infrastructure first, capacity later, and later rarely comes. Oloibiri ran the sequence backward. The training came first — before reliable power, before the data center, before any of it. And now the trained community is precisely what makes the infrastructure investable: a minigrid with a compute anchor and a resident workforce is a fundamentally different risk profile than a minigrid with a shipping container of machines and an absentee operator.

Mission 300 aims to reach 300 million people by 2030 with $30–40 billion in concessional financing behind it. The mathematics of that mission demand exactly what GEAPP’s authors called for: revenue models that reduce the subsidy per connection. We offered one version of the answer in 2022. The field validated the architecture. The market upgraded the tenant. And a village in the Niger Delta has quietly demonstrated the piece that makes it durable — the people.

I’ll be updating the full technical framework in a revised working paper. But the invitation comes first: if you’re working on minigrid finance, distributed compute, or workforce development anywhere in this ecosystem — I’d like to compare notes. The blueprint is open. It always was.

parts.label: Part Two: The People Who Proved It

paragraphs: I am not a doctor. I want to be clear about that before anything else, because in Oloibiri the line between 'the person who helps when you are sick' and 'a doctor' has become blurred by need, and I do not want to take credit for a credential I do not hold.

What I am is the person in this community who sits with you when something is wrong and does not panic, because I have learned — through hundreds of conversations with an AI that knows more medicine than I do — how to ask the right question slowly enough that we get somewhere useful.

sections.heading: Eight patients
paragraphs: This past week: a woman with fever and chills whose symptoms matched malaria closely enough that we recommended she travel to the nearest facility for a test. A man with a head injury from a construction site who needed to be watched for signs of concussion. A teenager with a wound that had become infected and needed proper cleaning and possibly sutures — we referred him and paid for the transport. A child who wheezed every night and whose mother had been told it was 'just his chest' for three years.

That child has asthma. His mother now knows what that means. She knows what to avoid and what to do in an episode and when to get to a hospital. That knowledge cost less than two dollars. The alternative — travelling to a clinic, waiting, being seen, being prescribed — would have cost a day's wages and a bus ride that most families here cannot easily afford.
I do not know if what I do saves lives. I know it changes what is possible inside a crisis.

chapters.title: He Had No Opportunity. He Had Everything Else.

paragraphs: Silas Clergy is 17. He is the oldest of seven children. His father collects scrap wood. Before the Davidson AI Innovation Center opened, Silas had no clear path to anything that required a keyboard.
Nine months after his first session, he had built ScriptureHub — a full-stack web application for scripture study, deployed to the internet, used by people outside Oloibiri.

I do not say this to perform amazement at what a child from a poor place can do. I say it because the narrative that 'these communities need opportunities' is precisely backwards. Silas did not need an opportunity. He needed a room, a screen, and an internet connection. He had everything else already.

sections.heading: The platform co-developer
paragraphs: Silas now co-develops nextvillage.community with me — the platform that hosts the vAI learning system. He works in React and Vite. He uses Supabase. He has designed features I did not think to design, because he understands what learners need from the inside.

He built an autonomous dashboard for community leaders that I had not asked for and had not imagined. He built it because it was needed. That is not a student following instructions. That is a developer solving a problem.
He is 17. He will be extraordinary regardless of what any of us do next. What we did was make the starting line visible.

chapters.title: A Teenager, a Notepad, and a Dying Cassava Crop

paragraphs: The Community Impact Challenge was designed with one rule: before you open the AI, you write down what you already know. You go outside. You talk to people. You come back with a notepad full of observations. Only then do you start the conversation with the machine.

The philosophy behind this is not anti-technology. It is pro-human. The AI is at its best when it is reasoning with someone who already has something to reason about. If you bring it nothing, it gives you its own assumptions in return. If you bring it a dying cassava field and the testimony of four farmers, it gives you a real investigation.

sections.heading: Godwill
paragraphs: Godwill Enoch was the first Community Impact Challenge champion. He chose to investigate a cassava disease that had been reducing yields in the surrounding farms. He did not choose this because he was told to. He chose it because he walked past those fields every day and had wondered about them his whole life.

He interviewed five farmers. He documented the pattern of spread. He photographed the discoloration. He brought all of this to the AI and together they built a diagnosis, a set of interventions, and a report that the farmers could use.

The Grand Challenge — three months of sustained, weekly engagement — grew directly from what Godwill showed was possible. The question was never whether the children could do serious work. The question was always whether we would trust them enough to let them try.

chapters.title: Brick by Brick - The Story of Bennywhite Davidson

paragraphs: There is a building going up in Oloibiri, Nigeria.
Not by a contractor. Not with a grant. Not with a timeline that anyone set from the outside.

Brick by brick, at the end of the day, after the lab closes and the young people have finished their sessions — they stay. They pick up tools. They move earth. They lay block. Not because anyone is paying them. Not because there’s a certificate waiting at the other end. They stay because this is their family, and the family needs more space.
That is what is happening in those photos. That is what it looks like.
Let me tell you how we got here — because the story of the Davidson Future Lab is really the story of one man who didn’t think of himself as extraordinary and turned out to be essential.

When I first reached out to Renewvia Energy about adding AI learning capability to off-grid communities they were electrifying, I wasn’t thinking about Oloibiri specifically. I was thinking about a project in Ozuzu, Rivers State. That community didn’t qualify. Bennywhite Davidson — Renewvia’s lead solar installer in the region — stepped in and said: I know a community. Oloibiri. Let me make this happen there.
He didn’t ask permission. He didn’t wait for a job description. He had a community he cared about, and he saw a door that might open, and he walked toward it.
That instinct — that particular combination of initiative and community rootedness — is what makes everything else possible. I didn’t know that yet. I do now.
The lab space itself is a good example of how Bennywhite thinks.

The original plan was to construct a small building specifically for the project. When he reviewed the costs, he made a different call: he repurposed one of his own storefronts — a provision store he’d been running — and converted it into the learning space. He told me he’d always intended to use it for something impactful. When this opportunity arrived, he knew.
He converted it himself, with community help. He made the renovation decisions himself. He redesigned the interior so the children would feel excited to walk in.

Then, when the space was ready, he went into the community and rang bells. Literally rang bells. Made announcements. Talked to parents and guardians. He understood that a lab without learners is furniture, and that trust has to be built before children will walk through a door and sit down at a computer for the first time.
Power came from the Renewvia solar mini-grid — intentionally, to demonstrate to the community what the grid was capable of. That decision was his too.

A lot of the operational energy and inspiration that brought the lab to life came from Samuel Adewumi. I want to name that because Bennywhite named it, and that kind of honesty about shared credit is itself a form of leadership.
Some of the donations go toward staffing. Bennywhite could simply hire one or two strong teachers and call it done. That would be the efficient management decision.
He doesn’t do that.

Instead, he distributes. He develops as many young leaders as he can — pulling them into teaching roles, giving them ownership, letting them grow into something. He knows who in that group came to the lab hungry. He knows whose family is food-insecure on a given day. And he does what he can — quietly, without making it a program — to make sure those young people know they belong, that they have value, that this family will not let them fall through.

That instinct — to sacrifice efficiency for development, to see a staffing budget not as a cost to be minimized but as a set of relationships to be cultivated — is not something you learn in a management course. It is what happens when someone who is deeply embedded in a community is given resources and trusted to deploy them according to what that community actually needs.
This is what I mean when I say Bennywhite has a community management intellect. He doesn’t optimize for the lab. He optimizes for the people.

But what happened next — sustaining the lab through early chaos, through technical difficulties, through a house fire that displaced Bennywhite himself, through all of it — that is Bennywhite’s doing. The data we collected over eleven months are unambiguous on this point: when he was absent, engaged learning dropped to zero. When he returned, the platform reached its single highest monthly total in the entire deployment. Technology constant. Community leader variable. The engagement tracks the person, not the platform.
I’ve written about that finding in an academic context. Here I want to say it simply: Bennywhite Davidson is why this works.
He once laughed when I asked how he became such an effective leader and manager.
“I’ve never been a manager,” he said.

He’s right. He hadn’t been. But like the young people who walk an hour each way to reach the lab — young people who had never touched a computer before they walked through that door — the fact that you haven’t done something doesn’t mean the capacity for it isn’t inside you. It means no one has given you the conditions to discover it yet.
That’s the whole argument of this work, if I’m honest. And Bennywhite proves it as much as any of the youth he’s brought along.
We now have more than 90 youth and young adults coming through the lab. We have 14 computers. The lab is open seven days a week. Some of the young people are walking an hour each way to get there.
They are coming for hope. That is the only word for it.

Bennywhite knows the space is too small. He knew it before the waiting list made it undeniable. So he did what he does: he started building. Not with a grant in hand. Not waiting for permission. He had been quietly setting aside a small portion of every donation — not enough that it diminished the lab’s operations, just enough that it accumulated — into a building fund.
And then he started laying brick.

The adults in those photos are community members who believe in what is being built. The children are the ones for whom it is being built — and they are building it too. Bennywhite’s wife, Confidence Onuhua, is there. His ten-year-old son, Onuhua David the Great, is there.
This is what community ownership actually looks like. Not as a phrase in a grant application. As people moving earth with their hands at the end of the day because they want something to exist.
I want to be transparent about my role in this, because I think the transparency matters.

I provided the initial capital — $5,000 of my own savings — and a platform. I have continued to make investments as impact became evident. But I am not in Oloibiri. I am not making the daily decisions. I am not the one who knows which families are struggling, which learners came without eating, which parents need a conversation.
Bennywhite is.

And so I made a decision early: the investments I make go to him. He decides how to deploy them. He is not accountable to me in the extractive sense of that word — he is accountable to his community. That is the right direction for the accountability to run. I trust him not because I have audited him, but because I have watched what happens when he shows up and what happens when he doesn’t. The evidence is overwhelming.

That trust is also a philosophy. I spent thirty years in engineering education telling students what to do and how to do it. I’ve spent the last several years trying to unlearn that reflex. The most important thing I’ve learned: it is better to be not in control. It honors the people who actually know the context. And it works better.
The building going up in Oloibiri is not a metaphor.

It is concrete block and red laterite soil and the hands of people who believe that what they are building together is worth more than any individual financial return to any one of them. It is Bennywhite Davidson’s wife and son working alongside community members at dusk. It is young people who came to learn and stayed to build.
When I watch those photos, I think about what it means that this is happening without me there, without my direction, without my approval.
It means it’s real.

chapters.title: Davidson AI Futures Lab in Oloibiri, Nigeria Is Writing the Future of AI
chapters.byline: By Kevin Patrick Hallinan and Confidence Onuoha and Silas Clergy

paragraphs: Oloibiri is the village where Nigeria’s oil age began. The first well was drilled there in 1956, and the wealth it produced flowed almost entirely past the people who lived on top of it. Seventy years later, three young people from that same village — and the surrounding Niger Delta network we’ve built through NextVillage — submitted entries to the Existential Hope Challenge, a global competition asking people to imagine a world meaningfully transformed for the better by AI by 2035.

As far as we’ve been able to tell, theirs were the only entries from Nigeria, and possibly from Africa at all. I want to be careful with that claim — I haven’t audited every submission — but if it’s even close to true, it’s worth sitting with. The challenge asked the world to imagine AI’s future. The people answering from inside the actual history of extraction, the actual texture of a grid that fails most days, the actual experience of governments and global capital deciding what their resources were worth without asking them — those people were nearly absent. Except here.
What follows are all three submissions, in full, exactly as written. I haven’t smoothed them.

Here’s what I want you to sit with as you read: eleven months ago, Silas and Confidence had never heard the term “AI.” Divinegift hadn’t heard it four months ago. None of them had written a line of code, touched a model, or imagined themselves as anything other than where they started — Silas selling timber, Divinegift navigating a village with no clear path forward, Confidence without the platform she now coaches from. Today all three are certified and proficient. Not curious about AI — fluent in it, fluent enough to imagine, in detail, what their communities could look like nine years from now, and to write it down for a global audience.

That’s the actual story here. Not just what they imagined, but how fast they became people capable of imagining it — and that the change they’re describing isn’t hypothetical to them. They’re already watching their communities improve.

sections.heading: I. Silas Clergy Idongesit, 17 — “Sacred Software: The Oloibiri Code”
paragraphs: Silas sold timber with his father before he ever touched a laptop. Eleven months ago he had never heard of AI. He’s now the senior developer and youth mentor at NextVillage’s Oloibiri hub, certified and shipping production code — and the person who taught a ten-year-old named David his first git clone. David is nineteen in Silas’s vision. He ships production code from the same lab where he learned to type.
World Name: Sacred Software: The Oloibiri Code
Name: Silas Clergy Idongesit
Your Role: Senior Developer & Youth Mentor, NextVillage Oloibiri. I sold timber here before I wrote code here.
Social Media/Website: scripture-hub.vercel.app | nextvillage.community

Vision Statement “In 2026 my family couldn’t afford the JAMB form. I had never coded until Davidson Innovative Lab. I sold timber with my dad. By 2035 I am senior developer of NextVillage’s Niger Delta network. David—ten when I taught him git clone, nineteen now—ships production code from that same lab. We didn’t wait for Nigeria to fix itself. We wrote our own software, in our own language, sacred and technical, on grids we built.”
Technology Offline-first solar AI with ScriptureHub: indigenous-language models for sacred and technical work.

Technology Description Nigeria’s grid fails most days. Ours doesn’t. Each NextVillage runs on solar micro-grids and peer-to-peer web mesh built with React and Supabase. Models live on the phones, not the cloud. When the national fiber went down in 2030, we kept teaching, kept worshiping, kept shipping code.

What kind of AI exists in your world? Three AIs run here. ScriptureHub speaks Ogbia, Ijaw, and Pidgin, switching between scripture and React errors. A grid optimizer powers clinics. A teaching companion lives on David’s phone. Last year, the translation model hallucinated a theological phrase during a lectionary update; the Elder Council immediately shut the model down for forty-eight hours until our youth patched the training weights. Tech serves the village; the elders hold the kill-switch.

New or Reformed Institution The NextVillage Digital Cooperative. Founded in 2028 when my mentors taught me that the cooperative would own the code, not me. The NVDC holds the grids, the models, the data. It is governed by voice-activated voting — important when half our elders never learned to write. Every decision about what the AI may say is made by people sitting together in a room. Mama Esther runs it now. She is sixty-eight. She has never coded. She has refused four foundation grants that came with strings.

Transformed Sector: Catechism & Code Faith, education, and software are one activity. A boy memorizing scripture also memorizes function signatures. A grandmother correcting the AI’s Ogbia pronunciation is also correcting its theology. David learned to code by maintaining our farm security and daily lectionary apps in the lab. First pull request at twelve. Pushed back on my code review at fifteen. Runs the youth cohort now at nineteen. There is no separate hour for prayer or work—we learn who we are together.

A Major Crisis Overcome: The Subsidy Collapse of 2030 Diesel hit ₦4,800 a liter in a week. Banks froze. By November, three hundred people walked into Oloibiri from Port Harcourt—families who had eaten last in shops they used to own. We fed them on stored cassava, slept them in the school, put the strongest to work on the grid. By spring they had built two more nodes. Some stayed. The wealth flowed the wrong direction that year, and we are still surprised it did.

sections.heading: II. Divinegift Morris, 21 — “NextVillage”
paragraphs: Four months ago — the shortest runway of the three — Divinegift Morris had never heard the term “AI.” She was walking by the Davidson AI Futures Lab and was curious. She entered and asked if she could ‘play’.  Of course, she was welcome. And she dove right.  She’s now AI certified and emerging as a communications specialist, while also successfully making her first changes to the nextVillage.community platform. She has been tasked - along with Silas - to add local languages to the platform.  The image below represents her vision for AI.

World Summary I’m Divinegift Morris from Oloibiri, NextVillage’s first AI Ambassador working in Community—the village economists finally learned to count. By 2035, 2,400 communities across West Africa run on shared phones and models we trained under Elder Councils, where children learn astrophysics in Ijaw as we transition from objects of study to primary investigators contributing original research.
World Name: NextVillage
Name: Divinegift Morris
Technology: Offline, multimodal edge AI with persistent memory, optimized to reason locally in Ijaw and Pidgin.

Tech Description This solves digital exclusion by running low-resource AI locally on old solar phones. In 2035, life is self-reliant: the Elder Council governs data, and locals are paid as primary researchers, not guides. AI assists daily, even watching a fishing net to teach the next generation.

Technology Description The breakthrough was small models that reason in low-resource languages. By 2030, compressed models ran on a five-year-old phone with a solar charger. By 2032, multimodal versions could watch a fishing net being repaired and explain what was happening. The models forget what we tell them to forget. They learn what the Elder Council approves. Outside researchers connect to ours — and pay our ambassadors as primary investigators, not as guides.

Which kind of AI runs in your world We use AI as a deeply integrated Tool AI, not an autonomous force—it acts as an extension of community memory and utility. It is co-built by local communities and tech hubs using 23 years of local data. Personal companions live on shared phones to tutor youth and help launch businesses. Ecological models protect our rivers by predicting floods and flagging oil spills, while cultural models preserve sacred oriki and fishing songs. The community owns the knowledge; the AI simply carries it.

Reformed Sector: Community The primary institution is the Community Sector. Its purpose is to measure, fund, and grow the uncounted local labor that makes society work—like grandmothers teaching river currents, elders mediating disputes, and youth caring for children. Once ignored, this formalized sector provides the economic soil for farming and weaving. Taught at UNIPORT and MIT, its ultimate purpose is to reverse the brain drain: paying youth to stay and build instead of leaving.

Transformed Sector: Community — Description By 2035, Community transformed from uncounted village labor into West Africa’s fastest-growing economic sector, scaling to 2,400 self-governed hubs. This matters because it democratized knowledge: hubs serving 240 locals daily operate entirely on local funding—costing just ₦200/month per household. By refusing corporate buyouts, we kept our identity intact. Our people are no longer objects of study; they are primary researchers with their names on the papers.

A Major Crisis Overcome We faced four barriers: no teachers, internet, tuition, or outside belief. We didn’t solve them; we dissolved them. We bypassed the teacher shortage by training 60 dropouts as Ambassadors. We erased the internet barrier by running models completely offline on shared phones. We eliminated tuition through local funding so no grant could cut us. Most importantly, we proved we were enough: Uncle Pere co-authored the 2033 IPCC paper, yet he couldn’t read English in 2026.

sections.heading: III. Confidence Onuoha — “Mutual Tide”
paragraphs: Confidence is the wife of Bennywhite Davidson, founding director of the Davidson AI Futures Lab, and one of the coaches in our lab, and — by her own framing — a daughter of the Sahel. Eleven months ago, like her husband and Silas, she had no exposure to AI at all. She’s now certified and coaching others through the same path she just walked, including her 10 year old son, David the Great, one of the most active students on the whole platform.
World Name: Mutual Tide
Name: Confidence Onuoha
Your Role: Policy Researcher and Daughter of the Sahel
Social Media/Website: nextvillage.community

Vision Statement By 2035, Sahel villages turn sun and seawater into food security. Smart microgrids and consensus-led Irrigation Circles replace aid dependency with local control over water, energy, and seeds — proving resilience can be built, not delivered.
Technology: Smart solar-desalination microgrids

Technology Description Solar-desalination microgrids turn brackish groundwater into irrigation water using only sunlight. Villages once dependent on erratic rain or aid trucks now farm year-round. By 2035, a family’s harvest depends on its own sun and soil — not a distant port or politics.

What kind of AI exists in your world? AI here is a Tool, not a decider. Soil-moisture and weather models were first built by outside engineers, for the community. By 2035, young people trained on the platform maintain and improve the code themselves. Ownership shifted from given to earned. Irrigation Circles still make final water and crop decisions, by consensus — the AI advises, it doesn’t rule.

New or Reformed Institution: The Sahel Water Commons A federation of village Irrigation Circles holds shared title to microgrid data and AI models. It sets fair-use rules for water, mediates cross-village disputes, and blocks any single buyer, corporate or government, from controlling supply. Power stays as distributed as the water it tracks.

Transformed Sector: Food Solar-desalination microgrids turn barren Sahel plots into year-round farms. Drought no longer means famine. Irrigation Circles set crop plans by consensus, prioritizing millet and vegetables over cash crops. Surplus is traded locally, not exported. AI predicts soil moisture, so no water is wasted. By 2035, food security means village control of sun, water, and seeds — not aid trucks, not corporate contracts. Just mutual harvests.

A Major Crisis Overcome The 2028 drought emptied granaries and tempted villages to lease land to foreign agribusiness for quick cash. Irrigation Circles refused, pooling solar-desalination units instead. Three dry seasons later, shared water held — proof that cooperation outlasted any single contract.

sections.heading: What ties them together
paragraphs: None of these three writers imagined AI as something that arrives and decides. In every version, a person or a council holds the actual power — Mama Esther with her refused grants, the Elder Council with its kill-switch, the Irrigation Circles voting by consensus. The AI does the watching, the translating, the predicting. The humans do the deciding. That’s not a detail any of them happened to share; it’s the one idea none of them could imagine a hopeful 2035 without — and it’s not a coincidence that the people least likely to romanticize AI’s autonomy are the ones who learned it most recently, on hardware that fails, on grids they built themselves.

And none of them imagined being given anything. Every crisis in every submission — the subsidy collapse, the drought, the four dissolved barriers — gets overcome by people building something themselves, often by refusing help that came with strings attached.

What strikes me most isn’t the visions themselves. It’s the distance each of them has already closed. Eleven months ago, Silas was selling timber and had no name for what a model or a kill-switch even was. Four months ago, Divinegift didn’t know what AI meant. Today they’re not just users — they’re certified, building production tools, training the next cohort of ambassadors, and writing nine-year visions detailed enough to submit to a global competition. The future they’re describing isn’t speculative for them in the way it might be for someone writing from a comfortable distance. They’re already inside the first chapter of it. Their communities are already changing — already improving — and what they wrote down is simply where they expect that line to keep going if nobody stops them.
In Oloibiri, a name is not only a label. It is often an assignment.

Parents give a child a name the child is meant to grow into — a description of who they are supposed to become, spoken over them before there is any evidence for it. The name arrives first. The person catches up.

Divinegift Morris is one of the leaders in our lab. Her mother tells the story that before the name, the baby cried constantly. Nothing settled her. Then they named her Divinegift, and, her mother says, it was as if the child simply became her name overnight. The crying stopped. She grew up into a young woman who is now a social media consultant with her own clients, an outreach director, and the person who has applied for consideration to present what we are doing in Oloibiri at an international innovation conference next year.
I am not offering that story as a scientific claim. I’m offering it as a description of what it does to a person to be told, from the beginning, exactly who they are expected to be.
David Onuoha didn’t wait to be told. He picked his own.
He chose “Great.” And nobody in Oloibiri calls him David anymore. He’s Great.
He is ten years old.

A year ago, Great had never touched a computer. Neither had any of the other young people who walked into the Davidson AI Futures Lab. There was no on-ramp, no keyboarding class in third grade, no laptop at home. There were four computers and about thirty kids who wanted them.

He is the son of Bennywhite Davidson, the lab’s founding director, and Confidence Onuoha, who is a nurse and the lab’s lead teacher. So you could say he had an advantage. What he actually had was proximity to two people who work relentlessly, and a decision to match them.
From the first weeks he was among the most consistent young people in the room. Not the loudest. Consistent — which is much rarer and worth much more.
When we launched the community impact challenges, Great looked at the leaderboard and did not find his name on it. He was disappointed. He sent me a WhatsApp message about it.

So I went and looked. He had a genuinely good idea. What he hadn’t done was go to an actual person in the community and demonstrate that the idea helped them. That’s the whole hinge of the thing — impact isn’t impact until someone else has felt it — and it’s entirely possible we hadn’t made that clear enough.

I want to name what he did there, because it’s the part that gets skipped in these stories. A ten-year-old who felt overlooked did not sulk and did not quit. He asked. That is a skill, and most adults don’t have it.
About three months ago, Great told me he wanted to learn to build a web platform.
I did not understand how serious he was.

He started using AI to help him, and he struggled. Then he struggled again. And with every struggle, something stuck. He learned what an API key is, and how to get one, and why you don’t hand it to strangers. He learned that a web page has anatomy — navigation, header, hero section, services, content, footer — and that those pieces are choices, not decoration.

He didn’t just build a platform. He built one he could use himself, to teach himself how to use AI. And then he opened it to other people so it could teach them too. He wanted it agentified, with a chatbot in it, because he had decided that a site you can only read is not as good as a site you can talk to.
He called it AI World. The tagline is his: Learn. Create. Explore AI.

He worked out on his own that Claude would help him think it through, and that Manus would get him to a live site faster. That trade cost him some control over the design. He made the trade anyway, with his eyes open, and he shipped.
He was proud. He should be.
Here it is, live, built by a ten-year-old who had never touched a computer twelve months ago: aiworld-bahkks2x.manus.space
Then he sent me the link, and immediately after it, this:
“Please, sir, if I have any mistakes, please correct me.”
I wrote back: Ok “Great.” What you have done is GREAT!
And then I gave him notes, because he asked for them and because he’d earned real ones:
The chatbot’s answers come back as one giant bolded run-on sentence. Give each new thought its own line. Bold is for emphasis — if everything is bold, nothing is.
The chat window is too narrow. Give it about half the screen.
And then the one that actually mattered: go through every page as a user would. Better still, ask Claude to review your site from the user’s point of view and tell you what to change.
That last suggestion is the whole game, and it isn’t really about web design. It’s the move from I made this to this is for someone.
Later I got on a voice call with Great and his mother, Confidence, and I asked him how many rounds of back-and-forth it had taken to build his site.
“Four.”
Then I asked him to guess how many changes I’ve made to the nextVillage.community platform.
He had no idea.

“About ten thousand,” I said. I was guessing. But it’s the right order of magnitude, because every single day for a long time has been one more small improvement. Fix a thing. Add a thing. Notice what a user tripped over and smooth it. That’s it. That’s the method. And it keeps getting better.

I did not say that to shrink what he’d done. I said it because I wanted him to hear that finishing is not the accomplishment — returning is. Four is not a small number. Four is where ten thousand begins.
Go visit AI World. If something in it strikes you — and something will — say so. He asked to be corrected, and he meant it.
A ten-year-old who has never owned a computer built a working, AI-powered learning platform in three months, and the first thing out of his mouth was a request to be corrected.
He named himself Great before there was any evidence.
There’s evidence now.

chapters.title: The Day We Got a Git Conflict

paragraphs: I was working on a feature for nextvillage.community. Silas was working on the same codebase from Oloibiri. We were six hours apart and had not coordinated well enough, and we got a merge conflict.

The merge conflict was not the interesting part. The interesting part was what happened when I messaged him about it: he had already identified it, already understood what had happened, and had a solution that was better than mine.

We resolved it together in forty minutes. This is the kind of thing that happens between developers. What made it remarkable was that six months earlier, Silas had never used version control. The projection had been eighteen months to this level of autonomy. We were at six.

sections.heading: AI as accelerant
paragraphs: The mistake people make when thinking about AI in education is assuming it replaces the human effort. It does not. What it does is remove the lag between when someone is ready to understand something and when they encounter someone who can explain it well.

Silas is ready to learn almost everything almost immediately. The AI met that readiness without making him wait for a teacher who might never come, a school he could not afford, or an institution that would not look twice at a seventeen-year-old from Oloibiri.
The AI did not make Silas capable. Silas was already capable. The AI made the capability visible, and then accelerated everything that followed.

In the first month, the children typed slowly and asked the AI to repeat itself often. They were not sure what they were allowed to ask. One boy typed a question, deleted it, typed it again. I watched him do this four times before he sent it.

In the fifth month, I have transcripts of children redirecting the AI when it gives them an answer that does not account for the specific conditions of their community. One girl told the AI: 'That is for cities. We do not have that here. What do we do instead?'
I did not teach her to do that. No one taught her. She learned it by doing it, over and over, until she understood that she was allowed to push back.

sections.heading: What the room became
paragraphs: There are now more than one thousand people on a waitlist to join the programme. Adults come in the evenings. Children teach their parents. Two Anglican priests use the lab every Saturday — it is their only consistent internet access — to research and compose their sermons.

The village elders issued a decree. I did not ask them to do this. They decided, among themselves, that every household should have at least one person learning at the centre. They announced it at a community meeting. I heard about it afterward.
I think about the first month often. I think about the boy who deleted his question four times. He is now one of our mentors.

I am an engineer. I track things. Here is what I can say with the data we have, stated as precisely as I can manage given that we have no control group and our sample size is still small enough that I am careful about the word 'proves.'

From month one to month five, clarifying questions from the AI to the learner declined by 71%. The AI needed to redirect the conversation less and less, because the learners were directing it better and better. This is the metric I care about most: not what the AI can do, but whether the human is taking over.

sections.heading: The numbers
paragraphs: Multi-step reasoning in learner sessions increased 52%. Verification language — learners checking what the AI says rather than accepting it — increased 212%. Structured thinking increased 88%.
88.9% of assessed learners reached proficiency. Eleven certifications earned. Four active community impact tracks: AI Ambassadors, Agriculture Consultant, Fishing Consultant, Healthcare Navigator.

Learners who had at least one human mentor logged 5.4 times more sessions than those who did not. This is the number I return to most often. The technology is necessary. It is not sufficient. The human in the room — Bennywhite, Michael, the peer mentors — is doing something the AI cannot do, and the data shows it clearly.

chapters.title: The Point Was Never the Certificate

paragraphs: Start with the room. Fourteen computers in Oloibiri, in the oil-producing heart of Bayelsa State, Nigeria. More than a hundred young people rotate through it. A year ago there were four machines and thirty kids. Graduates from that room are now in paid technical work. One trainee is a local nurse learning web development.
Most descriptions of a place like this stop at the training. Youth learn AI proficiency, youth learn to code, youth get certificates, everybody claps.
That was never the design.

sections.heading: The ladder
paragraphs: The nextvillage.community platform our learners work on has two halves, and only one of them usually gets talked about.

The first half is capability. AI proficiency — how to prompt, how to verify, how to spot bias, how to tell when the machine is wrong. Then the durable skills: critical thinking, creativity, communication, problem solving, digital fluency. Then real technical work — vibe coding, React, building an agent, building an agent that evaluates other agents. It is a genuine ladder and people climb it.

The second half is the reason for the first. Once a young person can work with AI competently, we hand them a tool that carries that competence to a neighbor who will never sit at one of those fourteen computers.

There are five such tools now: agriculture, animal husbandry, fishing, entrepreneurship, and a health navigator. Each runs in a browser, works offline and syncs when the network returns, and — this is the architecture, not a feature — coaches the young advisor instead of answering for them.

sections.heading: What “coaches instead of answers” means in code
paragraphs: Each advisor is a casebook. The agriculture page announces itself as “Your farmer casebook · Oloibiri & Ibiade.” A youth advisor doesn’t run queries; they carry a caseload of named people with open cases and follow-up dates.
Behind each casebook sit three separate AI prompts, and the order matters:

First, a probe prompt. The tool walks the advisor through a structured intake — for a crop disease that means crop and growth stage, exact symptoms, spread pattern, when it started and how fast it is moving, recent chemical applications, and the source of the planting material. Six questions, each carrying diagnostic logic. Spread pattern is not idle curiosity: patches suggest soilborne, a moving front suggests airborne fungal, scattered plants suggest an insect-vectored virus, uniform across the field suggests environmental stress.
When an answer is too thin, the AI does not fill the gap itself. It sends the advisor back to the farmer:

AI: So the disease problems are happening when the tomatoes are flowering. Are the flowers themselves being affected, or are the leaves or stems showing signs of disease, like yellowing, spots, or rot?
Farmer: yellowing
AI: Is this yellowing happening on the older leaves, the younger leaves, or all over the plant?
Farmer: all over the plant
AI: When the leaves turn yellow on all parts of the plant during flowering, do the yellow leaves also have spots, curling, or wilting besides the yellowing?
Farmer: yes
AI: ✅ This topic is well characterised. You can move on.
Fifty-one consultations in our records contain these probe exchanges. The AI is not diagnosing the tomato. It is teaching a fifteen-year-old how to interview a farmer.
Second, an advice prompt — the agriculture responses average about 2,900 characters.

Third, a follow-up prompt, which offers three things: explain the reasoning further, translate it into plain language the farmer will actually use, or handle referral logistics to ADP, NASC or IITA. The consultation record itself is designed to be read aloud to the farmer as a referral note.
And every session carries this, in the code, not the marketing:

This AI advice is advisory support only. For crop disease outbreaks: contact ADP and IITA. For food safety emergencies (aflatoxin): the produce must NOT be sold or consumed. The youth advisor must use their own judgement and training.
That last sentence is the whole thesis in fourteen words.

One more thing worth saying to anyone thinking about replicating this. The agriculture page is a hundred and sixty lines. It is a thin wrapper: it assembles a domain config — intake fields, prompt builders, categories, colors, offline tool — and hands it to one shared casebook component that fishing and animal husbandry also use. Adding a sixth domain is a config file, not a new application. That is deliberate. A village-scale advisory service that takes an engineering team to extend is not a village-scale advisory service.

sections.heading: What happened between May and August
paragraphs: Thirty-four young people logged 332 consultations between May 9 and August 25.
Two hundred concerned crops. Forty-seven concerned businesses. Thirty-two were health assessments, twenty-seven livestock, twenty-six fishing.

One hundred and ninety-six people are registered in the casebooks. They have names, phone numbers, villages, and a record of what they grow: cassava (36 farmers), rice (30), yam (28), maize (24), plantain, oil palm, cocoa. The fishing clients name their waters — Ikebiri Creek, the River Nun, Kolo Creek, Taylor Creek, the San Bartholomew. The business clients skew early: fifteen of twenty-five are idea-stage or under six months trading. Fashion design, food, phone repair, event catering.
They are not all in Oloibiri.
Ogbia, Nembe, Yenagoa, Brass, Otuabagi, Ibiade. One client in Abeokuta, four hundred kilometers west. Nobody planned that expansion. Word moved and the youth followed it.

The distribution is the Niger Delta in miniature. Crop disease, then pests, then soil and water — which here almost always means too much water sitting too long in the wrong place. Ninety-nine of the 332 consultations mention flooding, waterlogging, or the rains by name.

sections.heading: What it looks like from inside
paragraphs: The records are not tidy. They are better than tidy.
Here is an advisor chasing a pest problem down over six exchanges:
Advisor: how can i harvest crop when crops are eaten by pest.
Advisor: how can i identify the pest
Advisor: so after identifying this pest i will then use the neem liquid product right.
Advisor: if i want to buy five liters of this neem oil how much will it cost. Will the using of this procedure be hard.
Advisor: thank you for your advice on the use of this neem oil thank you so much may the god of abraham bless you

Read the fourth line again. She pushed until she had a price — ₦2,500 to ₦5,000 for five liters — because the farmer is going to ask what it costs, and “apply neem extract” is not an answer if you cannot say what it costs. Nobody taught her to ask that. The caseload taught her that the farmer would.
In another session, the AI kept addressing the advisor as though she were the farmer. She corrected it once. It missed. She corrected it again:
Advisor: No because i’m not he or his.
(the AI produces another script addressed to “Mr. Levi”)
Advisor: I am not MR levi, but a little girl of thirteen years.

A thirteen-year-old holding her ground against a language model that would not listen, mid-consultation on soil acidity and waterlogging. She finished the session and signed off: “good bye sir or ma.”
I taught engineering for four decades. I did not often see that combination of patience and refusal to be steamrolled.
And in a health assessment, the whole loop closed:

Chioma has peptic ulcer with gastritis. She has stomach pain, heartburn and vomiting. She said she buys drugs from the shop but it’s expensive. I advised her to go to the health center for proper treatment and to eat regular meals. She agreed to go to the clinic this week.
One record out of 332. It is also the only kind of record that proves anything — which brings me to the uncomfortable part.

sections.heading: We were counting the wrong thing
paragraphs: Our database has a field called resolved. Fifty-one of the 332 consultations carry it, and until recently I would have told you in good conscience that we had resolved fifty-one community problems.
We had not.

Forty-seven of the fifty-one have no recorded outcome at all — nothing on what the farmer did, whether it worked, or what it was worth. Median time from opening a consultation to marking it resolved: forty-five minutes. Thirty-one of the fifty-one closed the same day they opened.

The youth were not gaming anything. They did exactly what the button appeared to ask — the conversation was finished, so they clicked resolved. Nobody had told them the word was supposed to mean the farmer’s problem was finished. That is a design failure, and it is mine.
Four records in the whole corpus carry a real outcome. Three carry a number. One of the three is a failure:
the farmer washed cement bags in the pond and the fishs dyed
Five thousand naira of fish, gone. We logged it, which is the only reason I can show it to you.

sections.heading: Three more places the instrument was lying
paragraphs: The form was answering its own questions. Forty-four records — thirteen percent — contain no farmer information whatsoever. They contain our own help text, saved as though the farmer had said it:
Pest identity and management depends heavily on crop and stage — Fall Armyworm in maize whorl vs ear stage requires different responses.

Fifty-nine more are partly contaminated. One business client’s “business type” is a pasted Google summary of LLC tax structures. It is a single bug — placeholder text written into the value instead of rendered as a prompt.

Urgency was being read off the wrong thing. The tool infers urgency by scanning the AI’s prose for the word. The first check is a bare substring match on “URGENT” — which fires on any of three thousand characters of advice. Only seven of thirty urgent-flagged agriculture consultations actually contain an urgency header. One soil-drainage case was escalated to URGENT because the advice said “prioritized from most urgent to less urgent.” The same mechanism is why twenty-nine of thirty-two health triages came back RED and twenty-two of twenty-seven livestock cases came back emergency. No community caseload runs ninety percent emergencies. We were not measuring severity; we were measuring vocabulary.

And the referral loop never closed. The consultation record was designed to be read to the farmer as a referral note. In the health module, the referral note field is empty in all thirty-two records. Twenty-nine emergencies identified, zero referrals documented. Somewhere in there a patient age reads 2,015 years, because someone typed a birth year and nothing stopped them.

sections.heading: What we changed, and then the rains came
paragraphs: The community challenge now pushes for resolution. Not “did you finish the conversation,” but: what did the farmer do, what happened, and what was it worth? Outcome, narrative and value are required before anything closes. A RED triage will not close without a referral note. Urgency will be read from the structured header or not at all.
I expected the numbers to climb.

June was the peak — 179 consultations, 29 active advisors. August stands at 48 and 13, and that trajectory is not about motivation. When the rains are heavy in Bayelsa the lab is hard to reach, power is less reliable, and the fields and creeks the consultations are about are underwater. One follow-up note in the fishing casebook reads, in full:
check if the flood did not affect the fishing business

The conditions that make this advice most valuable are the conditions that make it hardest to deliver. We now have a better instrument and a slower season, and we will not know whether the new requirement works until the water goes down.

sections.heading: The number I will defend
paragraphs: Two hundred and twenty-nine of the 332 consultations are clean — real problem descriptions, real reasoning, a named person in a named community, produced by thirty-two young people. Sixteen of the thirty-four advisors worked across three or more domains, which means they are not running a script in one vertical; they are generalists learning to hold an unfamiliar problem.
So: 229 documented advisory encounters, 196 people, eight communities, four months.
Not fifty-one problems solved. I could have said that. The dashboard would have backed me up and no funder would have checked.

Refusing to say it is probably the more important output of this season. We built a village-scale advisory service staffed by teenagers, and the first thing it taught us was how easily you can measure the wrong thing and believe yourself. The young people came out of it more capable, and so did the people they served. The proof of the second part is what we are still building.
When the rains lift, we find out.

In a single week, 513 people walked through the Davidson AI Innovation Center and registered to vote for the first time in their lives. We did not plan this. We did not run a voter registration drive. A local official asked if they could use the space, and Bennywhite said yes, and people came.

I think about this number often, because it is not the number I was measuring. I was measuring learning outcomes and scaffolding rates and certification counts. I was not measuring civic participation. The civic participation happened anyway.
The standard narrative about voter disengagement in communities like Oloibiri is that people do not care. The data we now have suggests a different explanation: people did not have a place to go.

sections.heading: What eight months looks like
paragraphs: 42 active learners at the time of this writing. 578 total sessions logged. 66% of early learners expressed unprompted intention to teach what they had learned to someone else. Village elders formally encouraged all residents to learn AI.

The democratic exclusion thesis holds that low voter registration in marginalized communities reflects structural barriers, not apathy. We did not set out to test this thesis. We simply opened a room and kept the lights on, and 513 people walked in and registered.
I do not know what to call this. I know it is not what I expected. I know it is more important than what I expected.
I have never asked before. I am asking now.
For two years I tried to do this in Dayton, Ohio.

I had built the platform by then. It was good — better than good; it produced the best learning I saw in forty years of teaching. And I wanted it in the hands of the young people in my own city who get left behind first and helped last. That was the whole plan. Build the thing, walk it four miles across town, watch it work.
I went to charter schools. The administrators said yes. They said yes with real warmth, in meetings that ended with everyone agreeing this was important.
Then nothing happened.
Teachers would put a toe in the water. One lesson. One class period. A promising conversation in a hallway. And then the semester would close over it like water closing over a stone.

I am not writing this to blame anyone. Schools are carrying more than they can carry, and a retired professor arriving with a new tool is one more thing on a desk that is already full. But I want to be accurate: I could not move it. I am still trying. Beyond a summer camp for Black girls in Dayton, nothing stuck.
While that was failing, Oloibiri was happening.
I have called it a fluke. That is the wrong word and I want to correct it in public.

It was not an accident. It was being drawn down a path I would not have drawn for myself. Renewvia’s lead solar installer in Bayelsa State heard what I was proposing and told the people above him that he wanted the lab in his village. Nobody asked him. There was no role for him in any of it. He had a community he loved, he saw a door that might open, and he walked toward it before anyone told him he was allowed to.
His name is Bennywhite Davidson. For me there is a God connection running through the whole of it. I have written that story down at length elsewhere, so I will not relitigate it here.
Nigeria has a reputation. In tech it has a particular one, and it involves scamming. I asked Bennywhite about it directly and he told me the reputation is earned.
And then he went on caring about Oloibiri anyway.
He says of himself, “I am just a common person.” If the world were full of common people like Bennywhite Davidson it would be a substantially better world.
So Linda and I invested in him.

Four computers. That is what we started with in July of 2025, and that is what it stayed at for five months. Later we added ten Chromebooks. Chromebooks are what they are — three have already broken. Fourteen machines now, for more than a hundred young people.

Linda manages our money, because I am terrible at it. Left alone I would put all of it into this, and I would do it this afternoon. She grounds me. She has for forty-one years. And she still backs the craziness.
This particular craziness is working better than I imagined it could.

Two of our young people have been hired into tech jobs. I will be honest about my part: some of that came through an alum of mine, and Murali Kashaboina deserves the thanks. But nobody hires twice on a favor. They will prove themselves, and there are others coming behind them who will do the same.
They are not leaving Oloibiri to do it. They are improving the place they are from. Six hundred people registered to vote inside that lab. It has become the room where the town does things.
Here is the state of it right now.

It is rainy season, and this year the rain is worse. The solar and battery system cannot carry the lab through it. Which means that on the days the sky stays dark, more than a hundred young people who have organized their futures around that room are told to go home.
Three Chromebooks are dead.

And our community health navigator was mugged. He had just finished caring for a young person who might otherwise have died. They took his laptop. They took supplies. He came away despondent — a man who never imagined he would be allowed to do work like this, discovering that doing it makes you worth robbing.

He wants to keep going. He needs the laptop and the supplies replaced, and he needs a permanent place to work from — which is the new, larger space we are close to finishing. Room for forty computers.
We have fourteen. Ten of them work.
Faith is what Bennywhite and I carry in our pockets.
And I want to be careful here, because “we believe this should be happening across Africa” is the kind of sentence that costs nothing to write and means nothing to read.
So here is the version that costs something: it is already happening. We are opening in Osuzu, Nigeria, and in Sayanami, Ghana. Not planning to. Doing it.

That is not a vision statement. Oloibiri is eight thousand people on the ground where Nigeria’s oil was first discovered in 1956, and which the industry never came back for. Osuzu and Sayanami are next. Bennywhite will take it to the village after that.
Which is also the problem.
But I am one person. Two, counting Linda, and I could not do any of it without Linda.

I have applied for grants. None have landed. Our young leaders have entered challenges with real prize money attached. None have landed. Matthew O’Connell — my doctor for more than thirty years and, more to the point, my friend — funded the medical equipment that lets our navigator hand the AI measurements instead of guesses.
And the truth is that Linda and I are maxed.

I am taking consulting work in what is theoretically my retirement. Theoretical because I am improving nextVillage.community every day, ten and twelve hours some days, weekends included — while helping care for my eight-month-old granddaughters here in Seattle, where we are living with our daughter. I am sixty-seven. I am not complaining. I have never been happier in my working life.

But we can give a fixed amount each year, and we are at it. And every week the need grows. Bennywhite and Confidence — his wife, and the lead mentor for the young Oloibirians — ask carefully and humbly, and always for the same three things.
Sir, they say. I have told them I prefer mentor. Much prefer it.
A solar and battery system. Thirty more laptops. And more than $20 a month for the people teaching a hundred young people how to work with AI.
Twenty dollars a month. I want that number to sit there for a second.
So: I am asking. And because I would rather be specific than moving, here is exactly what things cost.
$150 — one Chromebook. One more young person in the room instead of waiting behind someone’s chair. We need thirty. We have lost three.

$1,000 — a solar and battery system. This one is the best deal in the whole enterprise. It roughly doubles the hours the lab can run, because right now the rain simply switches us off. A thousand dollars buys back half of a year.
$240 — one mentor, for a full year, at what we can currently afford to pay them. Read that again too. We would like to stop being a place that pays that.
Any amount. Any of it goes to work within the week.

I will not call this a donation, because it isn’t one. A donation is something you hand to people who need. This is capital placed with people who have been exploited for seventy years and are now building the thing themselves, on their own ground, under their own leadership, with an eight-thousand-person town watching them do it.
There is a difference between funding a need and investing in a capacity.
I have never made this request before. I have never had to.
If any of it reaches you — in your head, your heart, or wherever it is that decisions like this actually get made — please write to me directly:
kevin.hallinan@nextVillage.community

I am asking you to email rather than click a button for a plain reason: the platforms take about ten percent, and ten percent of a thousand dollars is a solar controller. Write to me and I will tell you exactly where it goes and then tell you what it did.
Every dollar goes to Bennywhite. Bennywhite decides.
Six months ago, Silas Clergy had never touched a computer.
He had a high school equivalency and no visible path past it. What he had instead was a thirst to learn and a quiet, stubborn commitment to becoming better than he was.

Last month he accepted an internship with a Nigerian technology company — one building B2B systems for restaurant and retail clients in both the United States and Nigeria, with the stated ambition of becoming the largest technology company on the continent. Not the largest in Bayelsa State. Not the largest in Nigeria. The largest in Africa. Competing with Tesla, with Google.
Why not.

sections.heading: What “learned to code” actually means here
paragraphs: That phrase is doing too little work, so let me be specific about the six months.
He built his own AI-agentified platform — Scripture Hub — where a user can hold a real conversation with an AI expert on the Bible. His idea. His architecture. His deployment. Nobody assigned it.

He develops on nextVillage.community through a GitHub team process: branches, pull requests, review, merge. The same way any professional team anywhere ships software. He fixes what’s broken. He builds what’s missing. Two of his features are live right now — a far better tool for administrators to see how their learners are actually progressing, and Nigerian Pidgin voice-to-text and voice output, so that a young person in Oloibiri can speak to the platform in the language they think in.
Think about that second one for a moment. That feature could not have come from me. I don’t have the language, and I don’t have the ear. It came from someone who needed it.

He learned data analysis end to end — cleaning and filtering, model training, model testing. He built a Long Short-Term Memory deep learning neural network to forecast time-dependent variables, then tuned it for better results. That is not a tutorial exercise. Plenty of graduate engineering students have never built and tuned an LSTM.
And he trains others.

sections.heading: Why I’m no longer telling this as Silas’s story
paragraphs: I’ve written about Silas before. The frame was: extraordinary young man, no digital experience, becomes a developer. It’s a good story and it’s easy to file. Exceptional kid. Exceptional circumstances. Move on with your day.
Six months later I think that frame is wrong, and worse, I think it’s the comfortable one. Because if Silas is an anomaly, nothing is required of anyone.
Here is what’s behind him.

A young woman now runs social media for nextVillage.community. She didn’t just take the job — she wrote code that scours social platforms every day for news about AI education in Africa, drafts responses she then edits herself, and posts them. She also writes her own pieces about what’s happening here. She built her own tooling for her own role. That is what fluency looks like.

A “next person up” team of four is in web development training right now, with AI as a collaborator rather than a crutch: two boys, ten and fifteen; a twenty-one-year-old woman; and the ten-year-old’s mother, a nurse. They are learning to use AI right — to work with it without surrendering their own thinking to it. That distinction is the whole curriculum, and it’s one most universities in the world have not figured out how to teach.
And that nurse is now designing the AI camp for eight- to ten-year-olds that will become the entry point for every learner who comes after — girls and boys both. I’m mentoring her. She’s building it.
We started last July with four computers and as many as thirty young people. We now have fourteen computers serving more than a hundred.

sections.heading: What the ceiling actually was
paragraphs: I spent nearly forty years teaching engineering. I’ve been in rooms where we discussed, with great sophistication, what students in under-resourced places were “ready for.”
Six months. From never having used a computer to production code, deployed AI agents, tuned neural networks, and a professional internship.

The constraint was never capacity. It was never talent, or hunger, or intelligence, or work ethic. Oloibiri has all of that in surplus and always did. The constraint was access — to machines, to connectivity, to someone who would take the first question seriously and then the four hundred after it.
Remove the constraint and this is what happens. Not eventually. In six months.

If that’s true in Oloibiri — a community in the Niger Delta that gave Nigeria its first barrel of oil and got almost nothing back for it — then the ceiling we’ve assumed for young people in a thousand other places isn’t theirs either. It’s ours. It’s an artifact of what we’ve been willing to make available, dressed up as an assessment of what they can handle.
That’s a harder thing to write than a feel-good profile. I mean it as the harder thing.

sections.heading: The Next Village
paragraphs: We built this to be handed over. That was always the point — not to serve a community, but to build a community’s capacity to lead itself, and then get out of the way of what it does next.
I can now say the thing I have been waiting years to say without hedging.
We’re ready for the next village.
And they — not we — have just started planting it.

Solomon Matthias Solomon, a resident of Oloibiri, gained AI proficiency skills through the Davidson AI Innovation Center. Now he is using those skills to conduct health triage assessments of community members who, like him, cannot afford healthcare provided by a local clinic.

chapters.title: One of the First in the World

paragraphs: The AI Healthcare Navigator created by Solomon Matthias Solomon may be one of the first in the world. It was enabled by the nextVillage.community platform. Mr. Solomon is bringing healthcare to people in his community who can't afford access.

This is what I dreamed about when I began developing AI Proficiency — and a lot more — with Bennywhite Davidson, the leader of the lab. My aim was to empower capabilities and opportunities through AI. I thought it would take a couple of years before the young people were ready to assume my role on the platform. In Silas's case, it took five months.
Silas Clergy, the 17-year-old Oloibiri youth who has made incredible gains this year, is now employed as an intern helping develop a digital clone of clients for a Nigerian B2B firm.

Metacognition is something you strive to develop in students, because you know how important it is for lifelong learning. My mentee Silas Clergy is now teaching others. But this story shows he is learning as he teaches. It's working.

chapters.title: Nearly Half of Them in the Rain

paragraphs: June to September is the rainy season in Oloibiri. When the sky stays grey, the solar panels don't make enough power, and a session that was supposed to run two hours runs twenty minutes. Sixteen young people earned their first certification anyway — after the rains started. Not the regulars adding to a stack. New ones, walking in during the worst months of the year and finishing something. Forty-one learners. A hundred and forty-five certifications. Nearly half of them earned in the rain.
This is where I would normally write a conclusion. I do not have one. The story is not finished, which is the only honest thing I can say about it.

What I can say is this: Silas will review my code before it goes into production. Solomon will bring the Healthcare Navigator to the next community when this model scales. Bennywhite will train the facilitators who come after him. I will fade from this work as it becomes something that belongs to Oloibiri, not to me — which is the correct direction of travel.

The cascade model works like this: the first cohort becomes the teachers. The teachers prime the next community. The next community produces its own teachers. At no point does this require a professor from Dayton. At no point does it require money that only universities have. At no point does it require anyone to wait for infrastructure to arrive before the learning can begin.
I want to end with something I have been thinking about since the first month, when a child leaned toward a screen and asked it if it could hear him.

It can hear you. That is real. But what matters — what has always mattered, what the data keeps pointing back to — is not the thing that can hear you. It is the person sitting next to you who decided to show you that you were allowed to speak.
A child whispering to a screen. Not the technology. The person. Always the person.
